source: NCERT Class IX, India and the Contemporary World I, History Ch. 4.

sections.heading: 1. Deforestation under Colonialism
points: **Deforestation** (clearing of forests) sped up under **British colonial rule**.

sub: Forests cleared for **commercial crops** (jute, sugar, cotton) and to feed a growing population.
Timber for **railway sleepers** and **shipbuilding** (the Royal Navy).
**Plantations** (tea, coffee, rubber) on cleared forest land.

sections.heading: 2. Scientific Forestry and Forest Acts
points: The British set up the **Forest Department** and brought in **Dietrich Brandis** as the first **Inspector-General of Forests**; the **Indian Forest Service** (1864) followed.
**'Scientific forestry'** — cutting old forests and planting **one type of tree** in straight rows (monoculture, e.g. teak/sal) for timber.
The **Indian Forest Acts (1865, 1878, 1927)** classified forests as **Reserved, Protected and Village** forests; villagers lost the right to use forests freely.

sections.heading: 3. Impact on Forest Communities
points: **Shifting (jhum) cultivation was banned**; hunting, grazing and collecting forest produce were restricted → **livelihoods destroyed**.
Forest people were forced to provide **cheap/free labour** for the Forest Department.
Anger led to **rebellions** — the **Bastar rebellion (1910)** in central India, and forest revolts elsewhere.

sections.heading: 4. Forest Transformations in Java (Indonesia)
points: The **Dutch** did similar scientific forestry in **Java**; the skilled forest woodcutters were the **Kalangs**.
The **'blandongdiensten'** system forced villagers to give free labour and buffaloes for cutting/transporting timber.
**Surontiko Samin** led a resistance movement (the **Saminists**) against Dutch control of forests.

sections.heading: 5. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Colonial deforestation for commercial crops, railway sleepers, shipbuilding, plantations.
Dietrich Brandis = first Inspector-General of Forests; 'scientific forestry' = monoculture plantations.
Indian Forest Acts (1865/1878/1927): Reserved, Protected, Village forests.
Jhum banned; forest livelihoods hit → Bastar rebellion (1910).
Java: Kalangs (woodcutters), blandongdiensten (forced labour); Samin's resistance.

sections.heading: 6. Common Traps (Watch Out)
points: **Dietrich Brandis** was the first **Inspector-General of Forests** in India.
**'Scientific forestry'** meant **monoculture** plantations, not preserving natural forests.
The **Bastar rebellion (1910)** was against colonial forest laws.
In **Java**, the **Kalangs** were skilled woodcutters; **Samin** led resistance.
